shots.title: Dallas, September 2000
shots.line: Dallas, Texas. September 2000. A meeting took place in this city that is now retold, again and again, as a business parable.
shots.src: Date and place as given in Marc Randolph, That Will Never Work (2019)

shots.title: Three visitors arrive
shots.line: According to Marc Randolph, a Netflix co-founder, three Netflix executives came here to meet the leadership of Blockbuster, the largest name in video rental.
shots.src: Marc Randolph, That Will Never Work (Little, Brown, 2019)

shots.title: The meeting room
shots.line: We have no transcript of that meeting. The room you are seeing is representative, and the people who were there remember the day differently.

shots.title: The proposal
shots.line: In Randolph's version, Netflix proposed that Blockbuster buy the company, and that the Netflix team run Blockbuster's business online.
shots.src: Marc Randolph, That Will Never Work (2019)

shots.title: Randolph's account
shots.line: Randolph described the meeting in his 2019 memoir. He recalls the price that was named, and a reaction he read as dismissive.
shots.src: Marc Randolph, That Will Never Work (2019)

shots.title: Antioco's account
shots.line: John Antioco, Blockbuster's chief executive at the time, disputes that version. In 2022 he wrote that no serious conversations about buying Netflix took place.
shots.src: John Antioco, LinkedIn post, as reported by Next TV, 3 June 2022

shots.title: The number
shots.line: The figure at the center of the story is fifty million dollars. It comes from Randolph's account, and it is where most retellings begin.
shots.src: Reported by Marc Randolph; not a signed or documented offer

shots.title: What really happened?
shots.line: Two recollections. One number. And a question that a single meeting, however famous, cannot answer on its own.

shots.title: Friday night
shots.line: To understand the decision, start with the business Blockbuster had built, and the Friday nights that built it.

shots.title: Inside the store
shots.line: Its strength was physical: walls of tapes and discs, new releases in bulk, and stores close to where customers lived.

shots.title: At the counter
shots.line: A customer chose a film, showed a membership card, paid at the counter, and promised to bring it back by a due date.

shots.title: An expanding network
shots.line: Repeated store by store, city by city, that simple transaction grew into a vast retail network.

shots.title: The scale
shots.line: By the end of 2004, the company described a network of roughly nine thousand one hundred stores around the world.
shots.src: Blockbuster Inc., Form 10-K for fiscal 2004 (filed March 2005)

shots.title: The rental model
shots.line: Every rental carried a due date, and every late return carried a fee. That small line on a receipt added up.
shots.src: Receipt values are illustrative

shots.title: Extended viewing fees
shots.line: The company later reported that those extended viewing fees made up about fourteen percent of its rental revenue in 2004.
shots.src: Blockbuster Inc., Form 10-K for fiscal 2005 (filed March 2006)

shots.title: A heavy business
shots.line: A system this large is powerful. It is also heavy, and heavy systems are slow to change direction when the ground moves.

shots.title: A new approach
shots.line: Netflix approached the same customer problem from the other side: a disc, a paper envelope, and a mailbox.

shots.title: In the mail
shots.line: There was no storefront. Orders moved through distribution centers, sorting lines and the postal system.

shots.title: The subscription loop
shots.line: Customers paid a monthly subscription, received discs, watched them, and sent them back. In this model there were no late fees.

shots.title: Two operating models
shots.line: Two businesses now served the same evening at home, for the same customers, with very different machinery working behind each of them.

shots.title: Cost structures
shots.line: One carried rent, inventory and staff across thousands of locations. The other carried postage, fulfillment, and the cost of winning subscribers.
shots.src: Conceptual comparison; not an exhaustive cost breakdown

shots.title: A growing online presence
shots.line: And it lived online, on early web pages and order forms, years before most viewers expected movies to arrive that way.
shots.src: Representative interface; not a recreation of any company's website

shots.title: Relative size in 2000
shots.line: In 2000, the difference in scale was enormous. Blockbuster was by far the larger company, and the more established brand.
shots.src: Relative scale only; not drawn to a numerical ratio

shots.title: Was the threat obvious?
shots.line: So was the threat obvious in 2000? Or does it only look obvious now?

shots.title: August 2004
shots.line: Blockbuster did respond. It moved into online rental, with a service launched in 2004 to compete directly by mail.
shots.src: Blockbuster Inc., Form 10-K for fiscal 2004

shots.title: Two systems
shots.line: Now it ran two systems side by side: thousands of stores, and a growing operation built around the mailbox.

shots.title: No late fees
shots.line: In January 2005, it made a major change. It stopped charging late fees at its company-operated stores in the United States.
shots.src: Blockbuster Inc., Form 10-K for fiscal 2004

shots.title: The financial impact
shots.line: The company's annual report for 2005 describes the financial impact of that decision, line by line.
shots.src: Blockbuster Inc., Form 10-K for fiscal 2005

shots.title: Costs and consequences
shots.line: The company reported that the program reduced rental revenues by more than five hundred million dollars, and cost about sixty million to market and implement.
shots.src: Blockbuster Inc., Form 10-K for fiscal 2005, Risk Factors

shots.title: Total Access
shots.line: In November 2006, Blockbuster introduced Total Access, its most direct answer yet to the mail-order challenge.
shots.src: Blockbuster Inc., Form 10-K for fiscal 2006

shots.title: Connecting the systems
shots.line: Online members could return a mailed disc at a store and leave with another film. For the first time, the two systems connected.

shots.title: Subscriber growth
shots.line: Subscribers grew quickly. So did the cost of serving them, and of the promotions that brought them in.
shots.src: Form 10-K fiscal 2006; first-quarter 2007 results release

shots.title: Growth and losses
shots.line: Growth came with losses. Attracting customers is not the same thing as making each of them profitable.
shots.src: Blockbuster first-quarter 2007 results release (May 2007)

shots.title: Three business models
shots.line: Retail stores. Discs by mail. Each with its own costs, its own customers, and soon, a third model that needed neither.

shots.title: Instant viewing
shots.line: In January 2007, Netflix announced instant viewing on personal computers, starting with about a thousand titles.
shots.src: Netflix announcement, 16 January 2007, and contemporary reports

shots.title: Early streaming
shots.line: It was limited at first. But it pointed toward a way of watching that needed neither a store nor an envelope.
shots.src: Representative player; not the Netflix interface

shots.title: A changing market
shots.line: Discs by mail, retail stores and streaming were now competing for the very same evenings at home.

shots.title: Rising costs
shots.line: Running a transition is expensive, and the cost fell on a business whose core revenue was already under pressure.

shots.title: Financial constraints
shots.line: Debt, liquidity and other long-term obligations left the company with less and less room to maneuver, and less time to adjust.
shots.src: Blockbuster press release, Exhibit 99.1 to Form 8-K, 23 September 2010

shots.title: The network dims
shots.line: The network that had been the company's greatest strength became harder and harder to sustain.
shots.src: Metaphor, not a literal closure sequence

shots.title: The bankruptcy filing
shots.line: On September twenty-third, 2010, Blockbuster filed for Chapter Eleven bankruptcy protection, a decade after the meeting in Dallas.
shots.src: Blockbuster Inc., Form 8-K, Item 1.03, 23 September 2010

shots.title: A quieter world
shots.line: Some stores continued to operate. But the dominant model of the neighborhood video store had faded.
shots.src: Exhibit 99.1, Form 8-K, 23 September 2010

shots.title: The meeting returns
shots.line: Which brings us back to the meeting in Dallas. A famous moment, and still a disputed one.

shots.title: What if?
shots.line: Could an earlier deal, different terms, or a partnership have changed the outcome? Possibly. None of these outcomes can be proven.

shots.title: Three converging forces
shots.line: The record points to something more complex: legacy economics, the cost of transition, and financial constraints, arriving together.
shots.src: Interpretive synthesis

shots.title: The evidence
shots.line: One meeting is part of the evidence. It is not the whole record, and it was never the whole story.

shots.title: The verdict
shots.line: Recognizing change is not the same as surviving it.

shots.title: Brand Coroner
shots.line: Every decision leaves evidence.
